Parcel Locker Network Optimisation

Central & Western District, Hong Kong: where to put parcel lockers, how many, and how big

Integer & linear programming · transportation model · queuing & Monte Carlo simulation · goal programming · decision analysis  |  Report generated 25 November 2026

Executive summary

Central & Western is home to 88,922 households (235,953 residents). We combined official census, building and terrain data with every existing SF Express, Cainiao and Hongkong Post (iPostal) pick-up point. We then used optimisation and simulation to answer three questions: where should new parcel lockers go, how many are worth building, and how big must each one be to avoid turning parcels away?

Key findings

  1. Today's lockers are badly placed for coverage. The 20 public lockers reach 37.0% of households within a 300 m walk. An optimal layout of the same 20 lockers would reach 82.5% (greenfield MCLP).
  2. 22 new lockers is the sweet spot. Coverage rises from 39.3% to 86.7%. After that, each extra locker adds less than 0.5% of district households. 13 lockers reach 80% and 30 reach 90%.
  3. Public sites alone cannot reach everyone. 11,208 households, mostly in the Mid-Levels and The Peak, have no shop, MTR exit or community facility within 300 m on foot. Public sites therefore cap coverage at 87.4%. Full coverage needs 97 new lockers, 72 of them in-building (estate) lockers.
  4. Coverage is not capacity. At an assumed 30% locker share, about 9,337 locker parcels a day are generated. Standard 80-compartment banks can absorb only 23% of them. Monte Carlo simulation (checked against the Erlang loss formula) shows the network needs about 14,080 compartments for ≤2% overflow on normal days and 25,920 for a Double 11 doubling.
  5. Targeted expansion beats uniform expansion. Placing 104 extra modules with a MILP serves 52.6% of locker parcels. Spreading the same 104 modules evenly (160 compartments each) serves 41.4%.
  6. Equity has a price. Coverage-only optimisation leaves The Peak at 0% and the Mid-Levels at 63.0%. Giving every area at least 70% coverage takes 35 lockers (14 in-building). Within a 22-locker budget, equity costs 11.6 points of district coverage.
  7. Build about 35 lockers. Under the base economic assumptions, expected value (EMV HK$2.42m/yr), Hurwicz, Laplace and minimax regret all choose "build 35". The pessimistic maximin rule picks "build 22". The expected value of perfect information is only HK$0.06m/yr, so the decision is robust and expensive market research is not justified.

1. Problem and approach

Hong Kong's e-commerce volume keeps growing: 49.6% of residents aged 15+ shopped online in 2024, up from 35.8% in 2018 (C&SD Thematic Household Survey). Doorstep delivery in dense, hilly districts is expensive and often fails. Self-collection lockers consolidate deliveries, but only if residents can reach one on foot, and only if the locker has a free compartment when the courier arrives. Our research plan therefore has four components:

  1. Spatial scoping and data: a census-anchored, building-level picture of demand and every existing and candidate pick-up location, with realistic walking distances on the pedestrian network.
  2. Integer linear programming: the Set Covering (SCLP) and Maximal Covering (MCLP) location problems.
  3. Stochastic simulation: overflow and service levels when compartments are finite and demand is random.
  4. Sensitivity analysis and managerial insights: walking radius, budget, demand surges and the economics.

We extend the plan with further methods from the course. Each is used where it answers a real question:

Table 1. Course methods and where they are used in this report

Course topic Where it is used Question it answers

Ch3.3 Goal programming Preemptive equity / coverage / budget goals (§8) Cost of serving the Mid-Levels and The Peak

All models are solved in Python with the open-source HiGHS solver (SciPy milp for integer programs, which uses branch-and-bound; linprog for linear programs, which returns dual values). The code, data and outputs are in the project repository and are fully reproducible (see the Appendix).

2. Study area and data

Study area. We use the official 2021 Population Census District Council District boundary for Central & Western (12.4 km² on Hong Kong Island; the uninhabited Green Island and Little Green Island are dropped). All 88,922 households and 235,953 residents from the 160 census Small Subunit Groups (SSGs) inside the district are included. Their totals equal the published district totals exactly.

Demand nodes. Demand is placed on 254 residential building clusters, not on coarse planning units, so that a 300 m threshold is meaningful.

  • Building footprints and storey counts come from the Lands Department.
  • Residential use comes from Buildings Department records.
  • Each SSG's census households are split across its buildings in proportion to floor area.
  • Student halls and elderly homes receive residents but no (domestic) households.

Supply. There are 156 existing pick-up points in or within 500 m of the district.

  • SF Express, Cainiao and JD points come from lists compiled from the operators' own sites, with coordinates.
  • iPostal stations come from Hongkong Post's official dataset.
  • 87 of these points form the public baseline (SF, Cainiao, iPostal). JD is kept for reference only, and residents-only lockers count for their own estate only.
  • There are also 445 candidate sites: MTR exits, supermarkets, convenience stores, malls, wet markets, community facilities and bus termini from OpenStreetMap, plus one in-building (estate-lobby) locker per demand node.

Walking distance. Distances are shortest paths on the OpenStreetMap pedestrian network (stairs, footbridges, lifts and the Central–Mid-Levels Escalator included), not straight lines.

  • Walking time uses Tobler's hiking function on the Lands Department 5 m terrain model, so uphill walks take longer.
  • Walking routes are on average 1.6× the straight-line distance. A Euclidean model would overstate 300 m coverage by about 180%.

Quality checks.

  • Operator coordinates were checked against an independent government geocode of their Chinese addresses: median gap 0 m on 130 sites.
  • Possible gaps in the pedestrian network (dead-end lifts, disconnected paths near homes) are listed for field checking.

At the plan's 300 m standard (about 4–5 minutes), only 37.0% of households have a public locker nearby. Counting staffed counters too raises this to 73.3%. Coverage is very uneven: Sheung Wan is well served, while the Mid-Levels (11.1%) and The Peak (0%) are almost unserved.

4. Location models (integer linear programming)

4.1 Formulations

Let \(I\) be the demand nodes with households \(h_i\) and \(J\) the candidate locations. Let \(d_{ij}\) be the walking distance and \(N_i=\{j\in J: d_{ij}\le D\}\) the sites within the radius \(D\) of node \(i\), so \(a_{ij}=1\) if \(j\in N_i\). Decision variable \(x_j=1\) if a locker is opened at \(j\). In the expansion models the existing lockers are fixed open at no cost. An in-building (estate) locker serves only its own estate.

Model A: Set Covering (SCLP)

$$\min \sum_{j\in J} c_j x_j$$ $$\text{s.t.}\ \sum_{j\in N_i} x_j \ge 1 \quad \forall i\in I$$ $$x_j\in\{0,1\}$$

The minimum number of lockers (\(c_j=1\)) such that every household has one within \(D\).

Model B: Maximal Covering (MCLP)

$$\max \sum_{i\in I} h_i y_i$$ $$\text{s.t.}\ y_i \le \sum_{j\in N_i} x_j\ \ \forall i,\qquad \sum_{j\in J} x_j \le P$$ $$x_j\in\{0,1\},\ 0\le y_i\le 1$$

The most households covered with a budget of \(P\) new lockers.

Both are 0-1 integer programs, solved by branch-and-bound (Ch3). We also solve their LP relaxations (\(0\le x_j\le 1\)) to measure the integrality gap.

4.2 Set covering: how many lockers for 100% coverage?

Table 4. SCLP at D = 300 m

Model New lockers Public sites Estate lockers LP relaxation Fractional x in LP B&B nodes Uncoverable nodes Uncoverable households
expansion, public sites only 31 31 0 31.0 0 1 66 11208
expansion, public + estate lockers 97 25 72 97.0 0 1 0 0
greenfield, public + estate lockers 100 31 69 100.0 0 1 2 897
  • Public sites alone cannot cover everyone. 31 new public lockers cover every household that any public site can reach. 66 nodes (11,208 households) remain out of reach: Central 117, Mid-Levels 7,911, The Peak 844, Western 2,336. These are hillside residential towers with no shop, MTR exit or community facility within 300 m on foot.
  • Full coverage needs in-building lockers. 97 new lockers (25 public + 72 estate) cover every household. Most of the estate lockers each serve a single tower cluster, so the last 13% of households costs about three times as many lockers as the first 87%.
  • The existing network helps, but only a little. Building from scratch would need 100 lockers, only 3 more.

4.3 Maximal covering: what does each locker buy?

  • The first lockers do the most work. The first 5 new lockers add 26.3% coverage.
  • The curve flattens quickly. By the elbow (P* = 22, 86.7%), each extra locker adds less than 0.5% of district households.
  • Higher targets get expensive. 80%, 90% and 95% coverage need 13, 30 and 51 new lockers respectively.
  • Public sites plateau. With public sites only, the curve stops at 87.4%.
  • Today's layout is inefficient. Today's 20 lockers sit far below what 20 optimally placed lockers reach (82.5%). Many existing SF lockers are clustered in Sheung Wan and Sai Ying Pun, within a few hundred metres of each other.

The LP relaxations of both models solved integral at every budget we tried, so branch-and-bound finished at the root node with zero gap. This is common for covering problems on real geography: the coverage matrix is nearly an interval matrix (lockers cover contiguous stretches of streets), which makes the LP polytope nearly integral. Simply rounding an LP solution is not safe in general (see the Harrison Electric example in Ch3). Here the LP bound certifies that the integer solutions are optimal.

5.3 Demand, surge and economics

Demand surges (+50%, +100%), parcel rates (0.20–0.50 per household per day) and locker shares (15–45%) are tested in the simulation (§7.5). The cost and saving assumptions are tested in the decision analysis (§9).

6. Capacity: a transportation LP with duals

Covering models assume a locker never fills up. To test this, we send each node's daily locker-bound parcels \(s_i = h_i\times 0.35\times 0.30\) through the recommended network as a transportation problem (Ch4).

  • Lockers are destinations with capacity \(c_j = K_j/\bar T\). With \(K_j=80\) compartments and a mean dwell of \(\bar T=1.5\) days, that is 53 parcels per day.
  • Arcs exist only where the walk is at most 500 m.
  • Total supply far exceeds total capacity, so the problem is unbalanced. A dummy destination (door delivery or a staffed counter) at a penalty of 1,000 m-equivalent absorbs the excess.
$$\min \sum_{i,j} d_{ij} f_{ij} + M\sum_i f_{i0}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \sum_j f_{ij}+f_{i0}=s_i\ \ \forall i,\qquad \sum_i f_{ij}\le c_j\ \ \forall j,\qquad f\ge 0$$

6.1 Coverage is not capacity

About 9,337 locker-bound parcels a day are generated. 8,609 of them come from homes within 500 m of a locker, but the 52 lockers can take only 2,773 a day. The LP routes 2,138 parcels a day (22.9%) to lockers, with an average walk of 102 m. 37 of 52 capacity constraints are binding.

6.2 Shadow prices, RHS ranging and reduced costs (Ch2)

  • Shadow price. The dual value of a capacity constraint is what one more parcel per day of capacity is worth: here, the walking metres saved, which is about \(M-d_{ij}\). Every binding locker has a high shadow price, so one extra compartment anywhere moves a parcel off door delivery. The range of feasibility (RHS ranging, Ch2.4) shows how far capacity can grow before the shadow price changes.
  • Reduced cost. For unused routes, the reduced cost (\(C_j-Z_j\), the improvement index of the stepping-stone method) is how much shorter a route would have to be before the LP uses it. The smallest are about 1–2 m: near-ties between neighbouring lockers.

7. Stochastic simulation of overflow (Ch7)

7.1 Model

Each locker bank is a loss system. Parcels arrive, each occupies one compartment until collected, and a parcel arriving when all \(K\) compartments are full is rejected and redirected. The arrival rate \(\lambda_j\) of locker \(j\) is the locker-bound demand of every household within 300 m whose nearest open locker is \(j\).

We simulate 1,000 days, after a 30-day warm-up, following the five Monte Carlo steps of Ch7.

  1. Probability distributions. Daily arrivals are Poisson(\(\lambda_j\)), or Negative Binomial with the same mean and variance \(m+m^2/5\) to capture e-commerce bursts. Dwell time is 1 day (60%), 2 days (30%) or 3 days (10%), as in the plan.
  2. Cumulative distributions.
  3. Random-number intervals for each variable.
  4. Random numbers are generated by computer.
  5. Trials. Each morning collected parcels free compartments, new parcels fill free compartments, and any excess is rejected.

7.2 Analytic check: the birth–death loss model

The generalised Poisson queuing model (Ch7 supplement) with \(\lambda_n=\lambda\) for \(n<K\), \(\lambda_K=0\) and \(\mu_n=n\mu\) (each occupied compartment is "served" by its owner collecting) has the steady state

$$p_n=\frac{a^n/n!}{\sum_{k=0}^{K} a^k/k!},\qquad a=\lambda\,E[T],\qquad P(\text{reject}) = p_K \ \ (\text{Erlang B}).$$

This blocking probability is insensitive to the shape of the dwell distribution: only its mean matters. This gives an independent check of the simulation.

  • Standard banks overflow badly. With 80 compartments everywhere (the plan's "medium" locker), 75.5% of parcels are turned away, and 33 of 52 banks are full on most days.
  • Each bank can be sized precisely. Sizing every bank with the Erlang formula (confirmed by simulation) for ≤2% rejection needs 14,080 compartments in total. Bursty (Negative Binomial) arrivals raise this to 19,560.
  • Monte Carlo agrees with the analytic model. The simulation matches the Erlang formula closely: mean absolute difference 0.7 points, maximum 3.6.

Practical sizing rule. Because the simulation agrees with the analytic formula, operators can size a bank with an Erlang B table. Look up the daily parcels \(\lambda\) times the mean dwell, then pick the smallest \(K\) whose blocking is below the service target. No simulation is needed site by site.

7.5 Peak surge stress test (Double 11) and demand uncertainty

  • Normal-day sizing fails at peak. On banks sized for normal days, a one-week doubling pushes rejections to 44% of parcels during the surge.
  • Peak capacity needs nearly double. Sizing for a +50% surge needs 20,040 compartments, and for +100% 25,920.
  • Peaks should be met with temporary capacity. Permanent banks should be sized for normal days, with temporary pop-up modules or extended staffed-counter hours at the hotspots for Double 11 and similar sales.

8. Goal programming: efficiency vs equity (Ch3.3)

The MCLP maximises total coverage, which favours the dense, flat west. A planner may also want a minimum service level in every area. We add deviational variables and solve with preemptive priorities (P1 first; its optimum is then fixed while P2 is minimised, and so on):

$$\begin{aligned} &G_1\ (\text{equity}):& \textstyle\sum_{i\in g} h_i y_i + d_g^- &\ge 0.70\,H_g\quad\forall\ \text{areas } g\\ &G_2\ (\text{district}):& \textstyle\sum_i h_i y_i + d_D^- &\ge 0.90\,H\\ &G_3\ (\text{budget}):& \textstyle\sum_j x_j - d_B^+ &\le P^* \end{aligned}$$

  • The coverage-only plan ignores the hillside. The MCLP plan (22 lockers) leaves The Peak at 0% and the Mid-Levels at 63.0%.
  • Equity first costs 13 extra lockers. Meeting the equity goal first needs 35 lockers, 14 of them in-building lockers on the hillside, and also reaches the 90% district goal.
  • At a fixed budget, equity costs district coverage. Holding to about 22 lockers while putting equity first gives every area at least 70%, but district coverage falls from 86.7% to 75.1%.
  • The trade-off is now explicit. Management can choose a priority order knowing exactly what it costs.

9. Decision analysis: how much to build (Ch6)

Alternatives: build 0, 10, 22, 35 or 50 new 160-compartment banks (MCLP sites). States of nature: locker adoption is low (15% of parcels), base (30%) or high (45%), with probabilities 0.25 / 0.50 / 0.25.

Payoff: annual net benefit = 365 × saving per locker parcel × extra parcels served − annual cost per bank × banks.

  • Parcels served account for capacity through the Erlang loss model.
  • Saving per parcel: HK$5. Lockers save roughly 20% of last-mile cost (McKinsey 2024), applied to a door delivery cost of about HK$15–25.
  • Annual cost per bank: HK$60,000. This is a published break-even scenario of about €15k up front + €3.5k a year, annualised over 5 years, plus rent.
  • Both figures are assumptions and are varied below.

Alternative Maximax Maximin Hurwicz α=0.7 Equally likely Max regret EMV
build 0 0.00 0.00 0.00 0.00 3.13 0.00

Results:

  • Maximax → build 35
  • Maximin → build 22
  • Hurwicz (α = 0.7) → build 35
  • Equally likely → build 35
  • Minimax regret → build 35
  • EMV → build 35 (HK$2.42m/yr)

With perfect information the expected value would be HK$2.48m, so EVPI = HK$0.06m a year. That is the most worth paying for a market study or pilot to learn the true adoption rate, and it is small because the same decision is near-optimal in most states.

The recommendation depends mainly on the value of a locker parcel:

  • build 0 is EMV-optimal for savings of HK$1.0–1.5 per parcel
  • build 10 is EMV-optimal for savings of about HK$2.0 per parcel
  • build 22 is EMV-optimal for savings of HK$2.5–4.0 per parcel
  • build 35 is EMV-optimal for savings of HK$4.5–8.0 per parcel
  • build 50 is EMV-optimal for savings of HK$8.5–12.0 per parcel

Below about HK$2 per parcel, no expansion pays.

10. Managerial insights and recommendations

  1. Expand in phases, following the MCLP curve.
    • Phase 1: 13 new lockers take coverage to 80%. These are the steep part of the curve, mostly at supermarkets, convenience stores, MTR exits and existing pick-up shops in Kennedy Town, Shek Tong Tsui, Sai Ying Pun and Central.
    • Phase 2: extend to the elbow at 22 (86.7%).
    • Phase 3: if equity matters (or under the base economics, where EMV favours about 35), add in-building lockers on the Mid-Levels and The Peak, up to about 35.
  2. Reuse existing pick-up shops. 8 of the 22 recommended sites are existing staffed counters (SF stations, Cainiao 驛站, JD counters at 7-Eleven) that could add a 24-hour locker bank. That means a partner and premises already in place, and no new site acquisition.
  3. Fix the existing layout before adding more of the same. An optimal 20-locker layout would reach 82.5% against today's 37.0%. Several SF lockers in Sheung Wan and Sai Ying Pun overlap. Operators should relocate redundant banks to uncovered streets before buying new ones.
  4. Size banks for demand, not by default. A standard 80-compartment bank is far too small where the plan places lockers, because the busiest sites see 300–480 parcels a day. Use the Erlang B sizing rule. The network needs about 14,080 compartments for ≤2% overflow. Put modules where the transportation LP's shadow prices and the module MILP point. The busiest sites are SF locker · 1Q Belcher's Street (λ ≈ 482/day); JD counter (7-Eleven) · Kennedy Town & Mount Dav (λ ≈ 437/day); SF counter · 144-148 Belcher's Street (λ ≈ 430/day); MTR exit · Whitty Street (λ ≈ 421/day); 7-Eleven · Shek Tong Tsui / Sai Ying Pun W (λ ≈ 420/day).
  5. Plan for peaks with temporary capacity. Double 11-type surges need about 11,840 extra compartments for one or two weeks. Pop-up modules, longer staffed-counter hours and nudging residents to collect within 24 hours are cheaper than permanent over-sizing. Shorter dwell times (the empirical 84%-within-24-hours pattern) cut the requirement to 11,760 compartments.
  6. Plan hilly districts in walking time, not distance. On slopes, a 300 m distance standard overstates service. Only 6 of 22 sites survive a switch to a time standard, and the Mid-Levels look much worse.
  7. The investment decision is robust. Most criteria agree on build 35, and EVPI is small. The key number to pin down is the operator's real saving per locker parcel, because that drives the break-even.

11. Assumptions and limitations

  • Demand. 0.35 parcels per household per day is about 350 M parcels a year ÷ 2.78 M households ÷ 365. The volume is a secondary source, while the household count is official (THS Report 82). The 30% locker share is an assumption (industry estimates 25–35%). Both are varied in Table 20 and §9. Parcel demand is allocated by floor area within census areas, and propensity to shop online is assumed equal across areas.
  • Capacity. Existing lockers are assumed to have 80 compartments (sizes are not published). Compartment size mix (S/M/L) is not modelled.
  • Behaviour. Residents use the nearest locker within the radius, and coverage is binary at the radius. A gravity or choice model with distance decay would be a natural extension.
  • Network. OpenStreetMap may miss some lifts, stairs and passages, which would make walking distances too long. Possible gaps are listed for field checks. The terrain model is ±5 m.
  • Economics. Monetary values in §9 are illustrative, anchored to published scenarios, and should be replaced with operator figures. Resident time savings and the environmental benefits of consolidated delivery are not included, so the payoffs are conservative.
  • Data. Pick-up point lists are third-party compilations of operator data (verified 2026-10-05). Cainiao's own figures suggest it has more lockers than are listed. Alfred24 was out of scope.

Appendix: reproducibility and data sources

Everything is generated by code in the project repository:

  • pipeline/01–06 build the data (download, demand nodes, supply sites, walking distance and time matrix, maps, quality checks).
  • models/m1–m5 run the models (location ILPs, transportation LP and module MILP, simulation, goal programming, decision analysis).
  • report/build_report.py writes this page.
  • models/run_all.py reruns everything.

The solver is HiGHS via SciPy. The simulation uses a fixed random seed for reproducibility.

Main data sources:

  • C&SD 2021 Population Census (Small Subunit Groups; District Council Districts)
  • C&SD Thematic Household Survey Report No. 82 (2024)
  • Lands Department building footprints and 5 m Digital Terrain Model
  • Buildings Department building records
  • Hongkong Post iPostal stations
  • SF / Cainiao / JD pick-up point lists
  • HKSAR Address Lookup Service
  • © OpenStreetMap contributors (pedestrian network, points of interest)

Literature for parameters: Urban Freight Lab locker dwell-time study (84% collected within 24 h); Australia Post locker dwell study (arXiv 2409.05061); McKinsey (2024) on out-of-home delivery economics; sciforum parcel-locker break-even model. All assumptions are listed in pipeline/common.py and models/*.py.

An interactive map of the data is in figures/study_area_map.html.
